subject: Copywriting
title: Anchoring: The First Number Wins
description: One-minute skill: Anchoring: The First Number Wins.

hook.text: Show someone $500 first, and $200 feels cheap. Show $50 first, and $200 feels expensive. Context sets price.

buildup.text: Tversky and Kahneman proved that the first number people see anchors all judgments that follow.

discovery.text: Pricing pages show the premium plan first. Your eye sees $299, then $99 looks like a steal. Anchoring at work.

twist.text: Anchoring works even when the number is obviously irrelevant. Random wheel spins influenced UN diplomats.

climax.text: Every 'Was $199, now $99' tag uses anchoring. The crossed-out price exists only to make the real one feel low.

punchline.text: The first number wins. That's why $199 is crossed out.

quiz.question: What is the anchoring effect in pricing?
options: The first number shown influences later judgments

details.summary: Anchoring bias means the first number people see sets the mental benchmark for everything that follows. A product priced at $997 'discounted' to $497 feels like a steal — even if $497 was always the intended price. Savvy copywriters use anchoring to make any price seem reasonable.
details.whyItMatters: Anchoring is one of the most powerful and ubiquitous cognitive biases in marketing. Understanding it helps both writers craft more effective pricing copy and consumers recognize when their perception of value is being manipulated.
takeaways: The first number presented becomes the reference point for all subsequent judgments
High anchors make lower prices feel like bargains regardless of actual value
Anchoring works even when people know it's being used on them

faq.question: Does anchoring work even when the anchor is obviously arbitrary?
faq.answer: Yes. In famous experiments, Daniel Kahneman showed that even random numbers — like spinning a wheel before guessing a country's population — influence estimates. The brain uses any available number as a starting point, even when it's clearly irrelevant.

faq.question: How is anchoring used in sales copy?
faq.answer: Show the highest price first (original price, competitor price, or value price), then reveal the actual price. The contrast creates perceived savings. Phrases like 'a $2,000 value for just $497' exploit anchoring to make the real price feel like a win.
